extracted.intended_audience: general news readers interested in business, corporate communications, and public relations
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of a corporate leader's public apology and media handling after controversial comments, focusing on who is addressed, whether responsibility is accepted, and whether the original statement is retracted. Useful for evaluating corporate apologies and PR responses to public backlash.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apology audience/scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Apology directed only to staff rather than the broader public or affected customers. ("has issued an apology ... — but only to his staff")
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An apology's intended audience matters: limiting an apology to internal stakeholders while leaving the public controversy unaddressed can fuel continued public outrage and may be seen as insufficient. Effective public-relations apologies often specify who is being apologized to and include the wider affected parties when harm was public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expression of remorse
rubrics_metrics.description: Spoken expressions of sadness and regret. (Quoted: "I'm sad. I'm really sad. I'm sad for the repercussions of my actions... I'm sorry to have put you through all this.")
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apologies should communicate clear remorse. Phrases that acknowledge emotional regret ('I'm sad', 'I'm sorry') are central to signaling contrition; however, sincerity is judged in context (scope, follow-up actions). Mere words without action may not satisfy critics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance of responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit statement taking responsibility for the impact of one's actions. (Quoted: "I take responsibility for all that has occurred and the impact it has had on you.")
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A credible apology typically includes unambiguous acceptance of responsibility for the consequences of one's words/actions. Vague or deflecting language weakens the apology. Corporate leaders should name the harm and own the role they played in causing it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retraction or failure to retract the offending statement
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the speaker retracts or stands by the original controversial claim. (Article notes he "did not retract his statement that 'some women's bodies just don't work' for his pants.")
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A full remedial apology often includes retracting or correcting the harmful claim. Refusing to retract while apologizing to a limited group can be perceived as contradiction or non-apology; communications should clarify whether the original statement is being withdrawn or corrected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public vs. private remediation
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction between addressing internal stakeholders (staff) and external stakeholders/customers who expressed outrage. (Article: apology to staff; "Some Vancouver customers still unhappy")
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective PR responses consider both internal morale and external reputation: private apologies may help employees, but public-facing remedies (public apology, product fixes, customer outreach) are usually required to restore consumer trust after public controversies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding blame-shifting in explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanatory comments that attribute product issues to customers' bodies/use rather than to the product. (Quoted explanation: "It's really about the rubbing through the thighs... how much pressure is there… and how much they use it.")
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When explaining product issues, avoid language that blames users' bodies, behaviors, or characteristics for defects. Such framing can be perceived as fat-shaming or victim-blaming; better practice is to acknowledge product limitations and describe corrective steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media-interview risk and channel amplification
rubrics_metrics.description: Controversial remarks made during a TV interview and then amplified online (YouTube) can rapidly increase backlash. (Article: comment made on Bloomberg television; video posted on YouTube.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spokespeople and executives must be cautious in live/media interviews; offhand comments can be recorded and widely shared. Communications strategy should include media training and rapid response plans for misstatements amplified by online platforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience reaction spectrum (critics and defenders)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public reactions can include both outrage and defense (some people criticized as 'fat shaming'; others defended his view that clothing can't fit everyone). (Article: "His comments sparked outrage... But others have come to his defence")
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or crafting responses, anticipate a range of reactions. Acknowledge legitimate criticism while understanding that some segments may defend the speaker; tailor messages to mitigate harm and clarify intent without escalating conflict.
